children.prompt: A kite is flying at a height of 45 m above the ground at the end of a string of length 70 m. Find the angle of elevation from the ground to the string, to the nearest degree.

spec.description: Horizontal ground, vertical height at the right, and sloping string; right-angle marker at the lower-right vertex. Decorative kite omitted.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 70 m; vertical opposite side 45 m; unknown elevation angle at the lower-left vertex.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and the unknown angle appear.

children.prompt: A kite is flying at a height of 35 m above the ground at the end of a string of length 60 m. Find the angle of elevation from the ground to the string, answering to the nearest minute.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\sin\theta&=\frac{35}{60}\\\theta&=\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{35}{60}\right)\\\theta&\approx35^\circ41'\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: The angle of elevation of the top of a flagpole from the ground, as observed from a point 15 m from its base, is $63^\circ$. Find the height of the flagpole to 1 d.p.

spec.description: Solid vertical pole on the left; dashed ground and line of sight to the observer on the right. Decorative flag omitted.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal distance 15 m; elevation angle 63 degrees at the observer; vertical height x.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens and the unknown height appear.

children.prompt: The angle of elevation of the top of a flagpole from the ground, as observed 50 m from its base, is $38^\circ$. Find the height of the flagpole to 1 d.p.

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\tan(38^\circ)&=\frac{x}{50}\\x&=50\tan(38^\circ)\\x&\approx39.1\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

children.prompt: The angle of depression from the top of a vertical cliff, 150 m above sea level, to a boat below is $50^\circ$. Find the distance of the boat from the base of the cliff to the nearest metre.

spec.description: Vertical cliff, horizontal sea-level base, upper horizontal reference and descending dashed sight line. Both right-angle markers retained. Scenery fills and decorative boat omitted; lower blue angle remains a permanent worked annotation.
spec.mathematics: Height 150 m; upper depression angle 50 degrees; corresponding lower angle 50 degrees; horizontal distance x.
spec.answerVisibility: The corresponding lower angle is visible only as part of this supplied worked demonstration.

children.prompt: The angle of depression from the top of a vertical cliff, 135 m above sea level, to a boat below is $37^\circ$. Find the distance of the boat from the base of the cliff to the nearest metre.

answer.worked:
The angle of elevation from the boat is $37^\circ$, equal to the angle of depression because the horizontal lines are parallel.
$$\begin{aligned}\tan(37^\circ)&=\frac{135}{x}\\x&=\frac{135}{\tan(37^\circ)}\\x&\approx179\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

inlines.text: A ship is 825 m from a 153 m cliff. Eric is at the top of the cliff looking down. Calculate the angle of depression.

spec.description: Cliff, ship, horizontal and vertical guides, line of sight, depression angle and two empty side-identification circles.
spec.mathematics: Horizontal distance 825 m; vertical height 153 m; theta is measured below the horizontal at the cliff top.
spec.answerVisibility: All response circles and calculation blanks are empty.

answer.worked:
The horizontal side is adjacent and the vertical side is opposite to $\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{153}{825}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{153}{825}\right)\\\theta&\approx11^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: A flying kite is attached to the ground. Its string is 45 m long. The kite is above a point 17 m away. Calculate the angle of elevation.

spec.description: Rising kite string, horizontal ground distance, vertical guide, right angle, theta and two empty side-identification circles.
spec.mathematics: Hypotenuse 45 m; adjacent side 17 m; theta is the ground angle of elevation.
spec.answerVisibility: No supplied answer or completed side labels.

answer.worked:
The string is the hypotenuse and the ground distance is adjacent to $\theta$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{17}{45}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{17}{45}\right)\\\theta&\approx68^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Evie is looking up at a plane that is a ground distance of 3.7 km away and is flying at a height of 800 m. Calculate the angle of elevation.

spec.description: Plane above the right ground point, rising line of sight, vertical guide, ground label, theta, two empty measurement boxes and two empty side-identification circles.
spec.mathematics: The ground box is for 3700 m and the height box is for 800 m; theta is the angle of elevation at Evie.
spec.answerVisibility: Measurement boxes and circles remain empty.

answer.worked:
Ground box: $3700\text{ m}$, adjacent. Height box: $800\text{ m}$, opposite.
$$\begin{align*}3.7\text{ km}&=3700\text{ m}\\\tan\theta&=\frac{800}{3700}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{800}{3700}\right)\\\theta&\approx12^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Jill is on top of a 75 m hill. The angle of depression from the top to the base of the hill is $37^{\circ}$. Estimate the distance Jill travelled to climb the hill.

spec.description: Terrain outline with straight base-to-summit estimate x, height 75 m, horizontal guide, depression angle, right angle and two empty circles.
spec.mathematics: The straight slope is the hypotenuse; the 75 m vertical side is opposite the 37-degree depression angle.
spec.answerVisibility: Unknown x and both response circles remain uncompleted.

answer.worked:
The vertical side is opposite and the straight slope estimate is the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{align*}\sin37^{\circ}&=\frac{75}{x}\\x\sin37^{\circ}&=75\\x&=\frac{75}{\sin37^{\circ}}\\x&\approx125\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Ted is looking up at a hot air balloon. The angle of elevation is $76^{\circ}$ and the balloon is above a point 460 m away. Calculate the altitude of the balloon.

spec.description: Balloon above the right ground point, dashed line of sight and vertical height x, ground distance 460 m, elevation angle 76 degrees, right angle and empty circles.
spec.mathematics: Adjacent side 460 m; opposite side x; elevation angle at Ted.
spec.answerVisibility: No numerical altitude or completed side labels.

answer.worked:
The altitude is opposite and the ground distance is adjacent to the angle.
$$\begin{align*}\tan76^{\circ}&=\frac{x}{460}\\x&=460\tan76^{\circ}\\x&\approx1845\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: Bec is set to walk a 165 m long tight-rope suspended between two buildings. The angle of elevation from the lower building is $23^{\circ}$. Find the distance between the two buildings.

spec.description: Two buildings on common ground, rising rope labelled 165 m, dashed horizontal separation x, elevation angle 23 degrees, right-angle marker and empty circles.
spec.mathematics: Rope is the hypotenuse; x is the horizontal separation adjacent to the 23-degree angle.
spec.answerVisibility: No completed side labels or numerical separation.

answer.worked:
The rope is the hypotenuse and the horizontal separation is adjacent to the angle.
$$\begin{align*}\cos23^{\circ}&=\frac{x}{165}\\x&=165\cos23^{\circ}\\x&\approx152\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The angle of depression of a boat at sea from the top of a vertical cliff $36\text{ m}$ high is $10^{\circ}$. Calculate the distance of the boat from the base of the cliff to the nearest metre.

spec.description: Vertical cliff on the left, horizontal sea-level baseline to a boat on the right, dashed horizontal reference from the cliff top and dashed descending sightline to the boat. No printed numerical labels or angle marks. The boat is an unfilled contextual outline.
spec.mathematics: The vertical cliff and horizontal sea level form a right triangle with the descending sightline. The angle of depression is measured at the cliff top from the upper horizontal reference.
spec.answerVisibility: No supplied answers or solution labels appear.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the horizontal distance from the base of the cliff to the boat. The angle of elevation from the boat equals the angle of depression because the horizontal lines are parallel.
$$\begin{align*}\tan(10^{\circ})&=\frac{36}{x}\\x&=\frac{36}{\tan(10^{\circ})}\\x&\approx204\text{ m}\end{align*}$$

spec.description: Observer at the left, horizontal ground to the building at the right, dashed ascending sightline to the building top, and a right-angle marker at the base. Decorative windows and doorway are omitted; the building remains an unshaded editable outline.
spec.mathematics: The building height is perpendicular to the horizontal ground. The sightline joins the observer to the building top. No lengths, angles or unknown labels are printed in the source diagram.

content.prompt:
Jack is on the top of a $65\text{ m}$ high cliff. He observes a man swimming out to sea at an angle of depression of $51^\circ$. Jack also sees a boat out to sea at an angle of depression of $30^\circ$.

Find, to the nearest metre, the distance between the man and the boat.

spec.description: Unshaded vertical cliff on the left, sea level extending right, two descending sight lines, and a dashed horizontal reference through the cliff top. The nearer sea-level endpoint is the man and the farther endpoint is the boat. Ordinary source colours are replaced by black.
spec.mathematics: The cliff height is 65 m. Depression angles from the horizontal at its top are 51 degrees to the nearer point and 30 degrees to the farther point. Endpoints are derived from these angles using horizontal distance = height/tangent(angle).
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated distances or final answer appear.

answer.worked:
Let $m$ and $b$ be the horizontal distances from the cliff base to the man and boat. The corresponding angles of elevation equal the angles of depression.

$$\begin{align*}
\tan 51^\circ &= \frac{65}{m}\\
m &= \frac{65}{\tan 51^\circ}\\
\tan 30^\circ &= \frac{65}{b}\\
b &= \frac{65}{\tan 30^\circ}\\
b-m &= \frac{65}{\tan 30^\circ}-\frac{65}{\tan 51^\circ}\\
b-m &\approx 60\text{ m}
\end{align*}$$

The distance between the man and the boat is $60\text{ m}$ to the nearest metre.

children.label: a
children.prompt:
A fishing boat starts from point $O$ and sails 75 km on a bearing of $160^{\circ}$ to point $B$.
How far east of its starting point is the boat, to the nearest kilometre?

spec.description: Blank four-direction compass rose for student construction; no journey or answers supplied.
spec.mathematics: North upward, east right, south downward and west left.
spec.answerVisibility: Student-visible scaffold only.

answer.worked:
The angle between the journey and south is $180^{\circ}-160^{\circ}=20^{\circ}$. Let $x$ be the eastward distance.
$$\begin{aligned}\sin(20^{\circ})&=\frac{x}{75}\\x&=75\sin(20^{\circ})\\x&\approx26\text{ km}\end{aligned}$$
The boat is 26 km east of its starting point, to the nearest kilometre.

spec.description: Completed southeast journey, full clockwise bearing, acute 20° reference angle, eastward unknown and right-angle construction.
spec.mathematics: Journey direction is (sin 160°,cos 160°); x=75 sin 20°.
spec.answerVisibility: Solution only.

children.label: f
children.prompt: Darius walked for 4.2 km at a bearing of $285^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ to a campsite. How far north of his starting point is the campsite?

spec.description: Unlabelled shallow northwest journey and acute angle arc from north; horizontal dashed leg and right angle.
spec.mathematics: Endpoint is (3 sin 285°, 3 cos 285°); acute angle from north is 75°.
spec.answerVisibility: Retains the source's unlabelled sides and angle.

answer.short: Reference angle $75^{\circ}$: H is the journey, A is the northward leg and O is the westward leg. $1.1\text{ km}$ north.
answer.worked:
Let $n$ be the northward distance. Relative to the angle from north, the journey is H, the northward leg is A and the westward leg is O.
$$\begin{align*}\theta&=360^{\circ}-285^{\circ}=75^{\circ}\\\cos75^{\circ}&=\frac{n}{4.2}\\n&=4.2\cos75^{\circ}\\n&\approx1.1\text{ km}\end{align*}$$
The campsite is 1.1 km north of Darius's starting point.

content.prompt:
A plane departed Sydney and flew due south for 350 km.
It then turned and flew due east for 500 km before landing on an island.
Calculate the bearing from the island to Sydney to the nearest degree.

spec.description: Sydney lies above an unnamed right-angle vertex; the island lies east of that vertex. Both named endpoints have N/E/S/W compass cues. Ordinary source colours are replaced by black.
spec.mathematics: The south and east legs have ratio 350:500. The requested direction is from the island northwest to Sydney. The supplied figure has no distance labels or bearing arc.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source givens are visible; no calculated angle or bearing is shown.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta$ be the acute angle west of north at the island.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta &= \frac{500}{350}\\\theta &= \tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{500}{350}\right)\\\text{Bearing} &= 360^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{500}{350}\right)\\&\approx 305^{\circ}\end{align*}$$
The bearing from the island to Sydney is $305^{\circ}$, to the nearest degree.

spec.description: Unlabelled right triangle with starting point upper left, turning point lower right and final point lower left. A dashed northward extension and clockwise exterior bearing arc retain the supplied 130° bearing.

spec.answerVisibility: The diagram shows only the supplied 130° bearing, 120 km distance and right-angle marker.

answer.worked:
Let $x$ be the distance south of the starting point.
$$\begin{align*}\theta &= 180^{\circ}-130^{\circ}=50^{\circ}\\\cos50^{\circ} &= \frac{x}{120}\\x &= 120\cos50^{\circ}\\x &\approx 77\text{ km}\end{align*}$$
Eleni is $77\text{ km}$ from her starting point, to the nearest kilometre.

answer.worked:

content.prompt: The bearings of towns $Y$ and $Z$ from town $X$ are $060^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ and $330^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$ respectively.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle XYZ with X below Z and Y, Z upper left and Y upper right. A dashed upward north ray starts at X. Only vertex labels are printed.
spec.mathematics: XZ has bearing 330 degrees and XY has bearing 060 degrees. Coordinates preserve the perpendicular rays at X and the 50-degree angle at Y without printing additional givens.
spec.answerVisibility: No answers, numerical angle labels or length labels appear in the question diagram.

answer.worked:
The angle between $XZ$ and north is $360^{\circ}-330^{\circ}=30^{\circ}$. The angle between north and $XY$ is $60^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle ZXY&=30^{\circ}+60^{\circ}\\&=90^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Given that town $Z$ is $80\text{ km}$ from town $X$ and that $\angle XYZ=50^{\circ}$, find correct to the nearest kilometre, the distance between town $Y$ and town $X$.

answer.worked:
Let $XY=x\text{ km}$. Relative to $50^{\circ}$, $XZ$ is opposite and $XY$ is adjacent.
$$\begin{align*}\tan 50^{\circ}&=\frac{80}{x}\\x\tan 50^{\circ}&=80\\x&=\frac{80}{\tan 50^{\circ}}\\x&\approx67\end{align*}$$
The distance between towns $Y$ and $X$ is $67\text{ km}$, to the nearest kilometre.

content.prompt:
Port $Q$ is 45 nautical miles from port $P$ on a bearing of $055^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$.
Port $R$ is 65 nautical miles from port $P$, and $\angle PQR=90^{\circ}$.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle PQR with a dashed north arrow from P, clockwise 55° bearing arc, supplied distance labels and a right-angle square at Q.
spec.mathematics: PQ=45 nautical miles, PR=65 nautical miles, angle PQR=90°. PQ follows bearing 055°T. R lies clockwise from PQ as shown in the source; coordinates derive from the given right triangle.
spec.answerVisibility: Only supplied givens are visible; the angle QPR and bearing of R from P are not labelled.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find $\angle QPR$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle QPR$.
$$\begin{align*}\cos\theta&=\frac{45}{65}\\\theta&=\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{45}{65}\right)\\\theta&\approx46^{\circ}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Hence find the bearing of $R$ from $P$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
The diagram places $PR$ clockwise from $PQ$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing of }R\text{ from }P&=55^{\circ}+\cos^{-1}\left(\frac{45}{65}\right)\\&\approx101^{\circ}\mathrm{T}\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A ship leaves port $P$ and travels 150 nautical miles to port $Q$ on a bearing of $110^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$. It then travels 120 nautical miles to port $R$ on a bearing of $200^{\circ}\mathrm{T}$.

spec.description: Unshaded triangle PQR with parallel dashed north arrows at P and Q, clockwise 110-degree bearing arc at P and clockwise reflex 200-degree bearing arc at Q. No side lengths or right-angle mark are printed.
spec.mathematics: P=(0,0); Q=5(sin110°,cos110°); R=Q+4(sin200°,cos200°). The leg ratio is 150:120. Bearing arcs run from TikZ angle 90° to −20° at P and −110° at Q.
spec.answerVisibility: Only source-supplied geometry, point labels and bearing labels are visible; answers and derived angles are omitted.

answer.short: $\angle PQR=360^{\circ}-(200^{\circ}+70^{\circ})=90^{\circ}$, using co-interior angles on parallel north lines and angles about a point.
answer.worked:
The north lines are parallel, so the angle between $QP$ and north at $Q$ is $180^{\circ}-110^{\circ}=70^{\circ}$ by co-interior angles. Angles about $Q$ sum to $360^{\circ}$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle PQR&=360^{\circ}-(200^{\circ}+70^{\circ})\\&=90^{\circ}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the bearing of $R$ from $P$ to the nearest degree.

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle QPR$. In the right-angled triangle, $QR$ is opposite $\theta$ and $PQ$ is adjacent.
$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{120}{150}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{120}{150}\right).\end{align*}$$
The bearing of $PR$ is clockwise beyond the bearing of $PQ$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Bearing of }R\text{ from }P&=110^{\circ}+\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{120}{150}\right)\\&\approx149^{\circ}\mathrm{T}.\end{align*}$$

spec.mathematics: Set T=(0,0), TD=40 on bearing 315 degrees, DC=sqrt(105^2-40^2) on bearing 225 degrees, and TC=105. Drawing coordinates use 2 coordinate units for 40 km.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Show that $\triangle TDC$ is a right-angled triangle.

answer.short: $\angle CDT=225^\circ-135^\circ=90^\circ$, so $\triangle TDC$ is right-angled at $D$.
answer.worked:
The bearing of $D$ from $T$ is $315^\circ$, so the bearing of $T$ from $D$ is $135^\circ$.
$$\begin{align*}\angle CDT&=225^\circ-135^\circ\\&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $\triangle TDC$ is right-angled at $D$.

content.prompt:
2 ships leave from the same port. One ship travels on a bearing of $157^{\circ}$ at 20 knots. The second ship travels on a bearing of $247^{\circ}$ at 35 knots.

(A knot is a speed of 1 nautical mile per hour.)

children.label: a
children.prompt: How far apart are the ships after 8 hours? Answer in nautical miles to 2 d.p.

answer.worked:
Let $P$ be the port, $A$ the first ship and $B$ the second ship. Draw the two routes with north arrows at $P$ and $A$.

The routes form a right angle at $P$ because $247^{\circ}-157^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}PA&=20\times8=160\text{ nautical miles}\\PB&=35\times8=280\text{ nautical miles}\\AB^2&=160^2+280^2\\AB&=\sqrt{104000}\\AB&\approx322.49\text{ nautical miles}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Calculate the bearing of the second ship from the first, to the nearest minute.

answer.worked:
The bearing of the port $P$ from the first ship $A$ is $157^{\circ}+180^{\circ}=337^{\circ}$. Let $\theta=\angle PAB$ in the right-angled triangle.

$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{280}{160}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{280}{160}\right)\\\text{Bearing of }B\text{ from }A&=337^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{280}{160}\right)\\\text{Bearing of }B\text{ from }A&\approx276^{\circ}45'\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: A plane flies 1200 km on a NE compass bearing and then changes direction to a bearing of NW and flies for 450 km.

children.label: a
children.prompt: How far, correct to the nearest km, is the plane from its starting point?

answer.worked:
Let $S$ be the starting point, $T$ the turning point and $F$ the final position. Draw the two flight legs and a north arrow at $S$.

The bearing of $S$ from $T$ is $225^{\circ}$, and the bearing of $F$ from $T$ is $315^{\circ}$. Hence $\angle STF=315^{\circ}-225^{\circ}=90^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}SF^2&=1200^2+450^2\\SF&=\sqrt{1642500}\\SF&\approx1282\text{ km}\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: What is the bearing of the plane from its starting point, to the nearest minute?

answer.worked:
Let $\theta=\angle TSF$. The final position lies to the north of the initial NE route, so subtract $\theta$ from $045^{\circ}$.

$$\begin{align*}\tan\theta&=\frac{450}{1200}\\\theta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{450}{1200}\right)\\\text{Bearing of }F\text{ from }S&=45^{\circ}-\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{450}{1200}\right)\\\text{Bearing of }F\text{ from }S&\approx024^{\circ}27'\end{align*}$$

content.prompt:
Checkpoint $C$ is due east of Checkpoint $A$.
The bearing of Checkpoint $B$ from Checkpoint $A$ is N$22^\circ$E and the bearing of Checkpoint $C$ from Checkpoint $B$ is S$68^\circ$E.
The distance between Checkpoint $A$ and Checkpoint $B$ is 42 kilometres.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Label the diagram and explain why $\angle ABC=90^\circ$.

spec.description: Unfilled triangle with A lower left, B above and to the right of A, C lower right, horizontal AC and a separate upward north arrow. Only vertex labels and N are supplied.
spec.mathematics: The schematic coordinates follow the stated bearings: AB points N22°E, BC points S68°E, and C lies due east of A. No numerical coordinate values are printed.
spec.answerVisibility: Question figure contains no distances, bearing arcs, angle values or right-angle marker.

answer.short: $AB=42\text{ km}$, $\angle BAC=68^\circ$ and $\angle BCA=22^\circ$. At $B$, $BA$ is S$22^\circ$W and $BC$ is S$68^\circ$E, so $\angle ABC=22^\circ+68^\circ=90^\circ$.
answer.worked:
Label $AB=42\text{ km}$, the bearing of $B$ from $A$ as N$22^\circ$E, and the bearing of $C$ from $B$ as S$68^\circ$E.
The reverse bearing of $A$ from $B$ is S$22^\circ$W. The south direction at $B$ lies between $BA$ and $BC$, so
$$\begin{aligned}\angle ABC&=22^\circ+68^\circ\\&=90^\circ.\end{aligned}$$
Since $AC$ is due east,
$$\begin{aligned}\angle BAC&=90^\circ-22^\circ\\&=68^\circ,\\\angle BCA&=180^\circ-90^\circ-68^\circ\\&=22^\circ.\end{aligned}$$

spec.description: Completed triangle with AB labelled 42 km, north directions at A and B, the south reference at B, bearing reference angles, interior angles and a right-angle square at B.
spec.mathematics: BA is S22°W and BC is S68°E, giving 22°+68°=90° at B. Interior angles at A and C are 68° and 22° respectively.
spec.answerVisibility: All added labels and construction marks appear only in the answer.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the distance, to the nearest kilometre, between Checkpoint $A$ and Checkpoint $C$.

answer.worked:
Let $AC=x\text{ km}$. Relative to the $68^\circ$ angle at $A$, $AB$ is adjacent and $AC$ is the hypotenuse.
$$\begin{aligned}\cos68^\circ&=\frac{42}{x}\\x\cos68^\circ&=42\\x&=\frac{42}{\cos68^\circ}\\x&\approx112\text{ km}.\end{aligned}$$
Checkpoints $A$ and $C$ are 112 km apart, to the nearest kilometre.

children.label: c
children.prompt: If a runner is travelling $12.6\text{ km/h}$, how long does it take her to travel between Checkpoint $A$ and Checkpoint $B$, in hours and minutes?

answer.worked: $$\begin{aligned}\text{Time}&=\frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}\\&=\frac{42}{12.6}\\&=\frac{10}{3}\text{ h}\\&=3\text{ h}+\frac13\times60\text{ min}\\&=3\text{ h }20\text{ min}.\end{aligned}$$

Finding: The worked examples depend on substantial right-triangle trigonometry prerequisites without an opening review.
Breakdown: Following the three examples requires identifying side roles, selecting a ratio, using inverse sine and solving side equations with the unknown in either the numerator or denominator.
Checked: All preceding teaching concerns angle interpretation and angle relationships. The immediately preceding topic and its supplied practice do not rehearse these trigonometric methods.

Proposed repair (add-review): Before p6-example-activity, add four short items within one page: (1) In triangle ABC, B=90°. Relative to A, identify AB, BC and AC, then complete sin A, cos A and tan A. [Adjacent, opposite, hypotenuse; BC/AC, AB/AC, BC/AB.] (2) Opposite side=8 cm and hypotenuse=13 cm. Write an equation and find θ to the nearest degree. [sin θ=8/13; 38°.] (3) Solve tan(42°)=x/18 to 1 d.p. [16.2.] (4) Solve tan(35°)=12/x to 1 d.p. [17.1.]

Finding: The reverse-bearing example uses cointerior angles without an opening rehearsal of that relationship.
Breakdown: Obtaining 116° from 64° requires recalling that cointerior angles between parallel lines sum to 180°. The worked caption names the relationship but does not rehearse it.
Checked: Earlier p4 teaching covers alternate angles, triangle sums and right angles, but not cointerior angles. The immediately preceding compass-bearing topic rehearses full-turn subtraction, so that piece has been removed from the finding.
Assumes: Cointerior angles are previously taught angle knowledge. No calculator is needed.
Proposed repair (add-review): Before p20-information-text, add three short diagrams of parallel vertical lines crossed by a transversal. In each, mark one interior angle and ask for its cointerior partner: (a) 64° [116°], (b) 105° [75°], (c) 132° [48°]. Keep the review within one page.

entries.description: Angles of Elevation and Depression

Angles of Elevation and Depression
• Line of sight is a straight line from your eye to an object.
• Angle of elevation: The angle you turn to look up from the horizontal.
• Angle of depression: The angle you turn to look down from the horizontal.
• The horizontal is a line parallel to the ground.

entries.description: True Bearings

True Bearings
Bearings: https://www.geogebra.org/m/er3jqacn
• Bearings give a travel direction from one point to another.
• With bearings, we are always taking a top-down view.
• True bearing measures the angle to turn clockwise from north.
• True bearings always use three digits.
If a navigator only hears two digits, then they know they need it to be repeated.
